extracted.intended_audience: Members of Congress, policymakers, and the informed American public
extracted.subtask_description: A 1953 presidential policy statement describing the Mutual Security Program: its purpose, categories of assistance, regional allocations, administrative arrangements, and the principles for deciding what aid to provide and how to provide it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy Purpose — peace through collective strength
rubrics_metrics.description: The policy is defined as 'the policy of peace through collective strength' — building sufficient military, economic, political and moral strength among free nations so they can deter and resist aggression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All forms of strength are 'indivisible' — neither military, economic, political nor moral strength alone will suffice. The goal is to enable free nations to stand on their own feet rather than 'carry the world on our shoulders.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Two broad funding categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Funds fall into two broad categories: (1) assistance to build up military strength of friendly nations (direct military aid and defense support) and (2) economic and technical assistance for underdeveloped areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amounts recommended: about 90% for direct military aid and defense support and about 10% for economic and technical assistance (fiscal year 1953 planning). The distribution rationale is explained in the program outline and table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct military aid vs. defense support (types of military assistance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct military aid = primarily military equipment and components; defense support = raw materials, commodities and machinery to enable countries to sustain and increase their military efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defense support should be used where it 'produces greater returns in military strength than would an equal amount of direct military aid.' Defense support is presented as an economical way to achieve mutual security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic allocation and regional priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: The bulk of direct military aid and defense support will go to strengthen the defenses of free nations in Europe; other allocations target Asia and the Pacific, the Near East and Africa, and Latin America.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific recommended amounts (as cited): military assistance for Asia/Pacific and economic/technical shares are specified (e.g., Asia & Pacific military/economic figures are given); recommended economic assistance in Near East $196,000,000, military assistance for Near East $606,000,000; Asia/Pacific military $611,000,000 and economic/technical $408,000,000; Latin America military $62,000,000 and technical cooperation $23,000,000. Europe receives the largest share overall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration and operating responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative arrangement: direct military aid administered by the Department of Defense; defense support in Europe and technical/economic assistance in Southeast Asia and the Pacific administered by the Mutual Security Agency; economic/technical assistance in South Asia, Near East, Latin America, and Africa administered by the Technical Cooperation Administration of the Department of State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These integrated arrangements operate under the Director for Mutual Security. Continue close coordination with international organizations and relate outlays to loans from the Export-Import Bank and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of assistance decided by cost-effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice between military equipment transfers and assistance in financing imports (defense support) is to be decided case-by-case on the basis of which form 'produces the most results in defensive strength at the least cost.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The program is planned so that assistance form is selected to maximize defensive strength per dollar; defense support is highlighted where it yields greater returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage European unity and self-reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. assistance should encourage accelerated progress toward European unity and the emergence of Europe as a self-supporting partner in defense of freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support steps such as economic cooperation, the European Payments Union, the Schuman Plan, and plans toward common armed forces, defense ministry and budget. U.S. policy is to encourage these developments in every way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating long-term dependency — enable nations to stand on their own feet
rubrics_metrics.description: The program is explicitly 'not a program to carry the world on our shoulders' but to make it possible 'for the world to stand on its own feet.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aid should be structured to help countries become self-sustaining in defense and economic terms rather than permanently reliant on U.S. support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point Four — principles for technical assistance to underdeveloped areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Point Four means making scientific advances and technical know-how available; it requires tailoring aid to each country's specific situation and is focused on training, demonstration, and supplying equipment/supplies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point Four operations must be supported by adequate supplies and equipment. Financing can come from private investment, export earnings, loans, or U.S. government aid depending on the country's capacity. Examples: India (large U.S. support for food production plan), Latin America (technical cooperation). Emphasizes multiplying effects of training and demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urgency and prioritization to prevent Communist gains
rubrics_metrics.description: Aid to underdeveloped areas must be carried out rapidly to prevent bitterness and frustration that could drive countries into alliances with Soviet communism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statement stresses 'speed in the interest...of the security of the whole free world' and calls for bold, timely investments before countries are lost to the enemy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link aid to concrete, sound local plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Assistance should support 'sound' and 'definite' local plans capable of producing concrete results (India's food production plan quoted as an example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference given to programs where local governments have practical plans and are financing significant portions themselves; U.S. aid supplements and accelerates proven national plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate with international organizations and financial institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mutual Security outlays should be coordinated with the technical assistance programs of the Organization of American States, the United Nations and its agencies, and related to loans by the Export-Import Bank and IBRD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maximize complementarity; encourage private capital investment to multiply impact and relate Mutual Security outlays to other public and private financing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance military and non-military measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Security requires military strength plus economic, political and moral strength; ignoring non-military dimensions would dangerously misunderstand the nature of the Soviet threat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs must invest in economic and political development, public health, education, and morale-building as integral parts of the security strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure efficiency in military strength per dollar
rubrics_metrics.description: Defense support is estimated to yield, according to the best estimates, 'more than twice as much military strength in Europe as would the same funds spent for the direct transfer of military equipment from the United States.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such comparative efficiency measures to decide whether to provide defense support (financing imports, raw materials, machinery) versus sending equipment outright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include limited assistance for special non-NATO or politically important cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Limited assistance is included for Yugoslavia (defiance of USSR), Austria (economic stability under occupation), and arrangements to facilitate emigration from Europe; arrangements with Spain are also expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are treated as special cases with tailored amounts and arrangements using funds already available or recommended by Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production and delivery timeliness for rearmament needs
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. must step up production and speed deliveries to equip forces raised by Allies; production delays and Korea combat requirements have affected deliveries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directives to accelerate production and prioritize deliveries for North Atlantic Treaty defense forces while maintaining Korea requirements as top priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigate European economic strains from rearmament
rubrics_metrics.description: Rearmament has imposed new pressures on European economies (price rises, balance-of-payments problems); U.S. defense support should provide the margin of raw materials and other support to allow Europe to sustain rearmament without collapse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defense support should enable Europe to use existing plants and manpower for defense purposes and prevent destabilizing economic consequences of rapid rearmament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor financing method to country capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Some countries can attract private capital or finance development from exports; others need substantial U.S. government-provided supplies and equipment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide financing (private investment, exports, loans, or direct U.S. aid) based on each country's ability to finance its development and on the likelihood of producing sound results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic assumptions and sustainability of domestic economy
rubrics_metrics.description: The national security program rests on projections that U.S. production will continue to rise, enabling the country to afford large security expenditures without crippling civilian consumption or investment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program justification includes macroeconomic forecasts (expected GNP increases) and the assertion that civilian consumption and investment can remain strong despite security outlays.
